Need to make the NA values true NA values so the string is read as a numeric rather than chr so that I can calculate means.

```{r str data}
  mutate(sed_dep1 = as.numeric(na_if(sed_dep1, "NA")))

str(dat)

```

Before making graphs I need to do some calculations.
Each site there were 3 replicates of sediment deposition tubes to get a mean of sediment deposition.
So I need to calculate the mean than find the deposition rate per area per time so I can compare it across sites.

```{r mean}
cols <- c("sed_dep1", "sed_dep2", "sed_dep3") #make a string to get the mean

dep_av <- rowMeans(dat[cols], na.rm = TRUE) #mean while ignoring the NA

dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    sed_dep_av = (dep_av/(Area * Time_elapsed)), #sediment deposition/cm^2/day
    sed_dep_sd = sd(dep_av)/(Area * Time_elapsed) #area and time are constants between the 3 sediment deposition used for averages thus there is no variance between them. 
  )
```

Currently, mussel, crab, and stem counts are referencing a 1/16 meter squared plot.For ease of comparison, I am going to extrapolate it to a meter square density

```{r meter-squared}
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    Live_count1 = Live_count1*16,
    Dead_count1 = Dead_count1*16,
    Mussel_count = Mussel_count*16,
    Burrow_count = Burrow_count*16, 
    Live_count2 = Live_count2*16,
    Dead_count2 = Dead_count2*16, 
    Crabf = factor(Crab),
    Musself = factor(Mussel),
    Treatmentf = factor(Treatment),
    Site_IDF = factor(Site_ID),
    Replicatef = factor(Replicate)) %>%
  mutate(
    Category = case_when(
      Crab == "yes" & Mussel == "no" ~ "Crab",
      Crab == "no" & Mussel == "yes" ~ "Mussel",
      Crab == "yes" & Mussel == "yes" ~ "Crab + Mussel",
      TRUE ~ "None"
    )
  )

print(dat)

ss_dat <- ss_dat %>% #need these as factors for making models later
  mutate(
   Crabf = factor(Crab),
    Musself = factor(Mussel),
    Treatmentf = factor(Treatment),
    Site_IDF = factor(Site_ID)
  )

```

```{r ss summary}

summary_ss <- ss_dat %>% #get means for simplicity of the plot
  group_by(Treatment, Vane_depth) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(Strength), 
            se = sd(Strength),
            xmin = mean - se,
            xmax = mean + se,
            .groups = "drop")%>%
  mutate(Treatment = dplyr::recode(Treatment,
    "cc" = "Crab Only",
    "mc" = "Mussel Only",
    "mcc" = "Crab & Mussel",
    "ncnc" = "Reference",
    "ncnm" = "Control"
  ))

print(summary_ss)
```

###Control to Reference Plot Comparisons
H0: Control plots are not different than reference plots for sediment depoistion or soil strength

If I fail to reject the null hypothesis I can remove refence plot treatments from my modeling analysis as there was no effect of the caging material on my desired response variables. 
```{r Mann-Whitney U, t-test}
#Sediment Deposition comparison test first
dat2 <- dat%>%
  filter(Treatment %in% c("ncnc", "ncnm"))

##Normality check 
ggplot(dat2,aes(x = sed_dep_av)) + 
  geom_histogram() + 
  stat_bin(bins = 10)+
  theme_classic()

qqnorm(dat2$sed_dep_av)
qqline(dat2$sed_dep_av, lwd = 2, col = "blue") #slight right skew 

##test
shapiro.test(dat2$sed_dep_av) #W = 0.85426, p-value = 0.01575, data is not normal so use Mann-Whitney U test

wilcox.test(sed_dep_av ~ Treatment, data = dat2) #W = 41, p-value = 0.3823 so I fail to reject the null hypothesis

#Soil Strength Comparison test, have to check at each depth interval to compare the two groups 

##depth 0-10cm
###Normality check
qqnorm(dat2$ss1)
qqline(dat2$ss1, lwd = 2, col = "blue") #dip in the middle  

shapiro.test(dat2$ss1) #W = 0.92816, p-value = 0.2279, data is normal so can use the two sample t-test

##test
t.test(ss1 ~ Treatment, data = dat2) #t = 1.1035, df = 12.098, p-value = 0.2913

##depth 10-20cm
###Normality check
qqnorm(dat2$ss2)
qqline(dat2$ss2, lwd = 2, col = "blue") #looks good 

shapiro.test(dat2$ss2) #W = 0.9652, p-value = 0.7561, data is normal so can use the two sample t-test
##test
t.test(ss2 ~ Treatment, data = dat2) #t = 1.39, df = 12.512, p-value = 0.1888

##depth 20-30cm
###Normality check
qqnorm(dat2$ss3)
qqline(dat2$ss3, lwd = 2, col = "blue") #looks good 

shapiro.test(dat2$ss3) #W = 0.98522, p-value = 0.9917, data is normal so can use the two sample t-test

##test
t.test(ss3 ~ Treatment, data = dat2) #t = 0.69953, df = 13.995, p-value = 0.4957

##depth 30-40cm
###Normality check
qqnorm(dat2$ss4)
qqline(dat2$ss4, lwd = 2, col = "blue") #slight deviations at end points

shapiro.test(dat2$ss4) #W = 0.98007, p-value = 0.9642, data is normal so can use the two sample t-test

##test
t.test(ss4 ~ Treatment, data = dat2) #t = -0.38713, df = 12.821, p-value = 0.705

##depth 40-50cm
###Normality check
qqnorm(dat2$ss5)
qqline(dat2$ss5, lwd = 2, col = "blue") #slight deviations at end points

shapiro.test(dat2$ss5) #W = 0.92715, p-value = 0.2196, data is normal so can use the two sample t-test

##test
t.test(ss5 ~ Treatment, data = dat2) #t = -0.15377, df = 13.295, p-value = 0.8801

#Bonferroni adjustment
##because I did 6 statistical tests with these two treatments I need to correct my p-value to alpha/number of tests which the new alpha would be 0.0083. This shouldn't be a problem because I am hoping for the null hypothesis
```
Conclusions: Based on the two sample t-tests conducted and the Mann Whitney-U test, the control and references cages are not different in terms of the two response variables: sediment deposition and soil strength. Thus, I can remove reference cages from analysis when considering my models and just have the controls against the other treatments. 

#Models 
##Q1
1.How does the presence of the fiddler crab, Minuca pugnax, effect salt marsh stability: resistance to erosion (quantified by soil strength as a proxy) and vertical accretion?

I am going to start with a general linear model even though the raw residuals were not normal to check is standardized residuals are. If the standardized residuals are not normal I will move to a generalized linear model if they are normal, I will continue using LMs. If I use a generalized linear model, because the data is continuous with positive values I will use a gamma distribution with an inverse canonical link. I will make models with replicate as a random variable to deal with the cages not being truly independent from each other due to proximity of all of the cages being in one site. 
```{r model}
#make new dataset without the reference plots
dat3 <- dat %>%
  filter(Treatment %in% c("cc", "ncnm", "mc", "mcc"))
hist(dat3$sed_dep_av)

#check for multicolinearity
GGally::ggpairs(dat3[,c(15, 29, 45)]) #not straight lines, so we are looking good here

#potential models

m0a <- lm(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf, data = dat3)
summary(m0a)#The standard errors look good as they are all an order of magnitude lower. The mussel crab cage and reference cage has a lower sediment deposition compared to the crab cage. The mussel cage has a higher sediment deposition compared to the crab cage. Multiple r squared is low (o.o4195), this currently doesn't really describe what's happening.
check_model(m0a)#Normality looks a little skewed at the extremes but nothing I am too worried about. The homogeneity of variance however, could be better so I am going to compared with a GLM

m0b <- glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf, data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m0b) #The standard error is high compared to the estimates. The estimates for all other treatments compared to cc is the same, which seems off

check_model(m0b)

#Continuing with gamma log link GLM
m1b <- glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf + Elevation, data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m1b)#standard errors are not better as they are still on the same order of magnitude, the elevation error is an order of magnitude less than estimate

m2b <- glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf + Elevation + (1|Replicatef), data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m2b) #random effect standard error is higher than variance. 

m3b <-glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf + Elevation + Live_count2, data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m3b)#Standard errors are still on the same order of magnitude for some values

m4b <-glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf*Live_count2 + Elevation*Live_count2, data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m4b)

m5b <-glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf*Live_count2 + Elevation*Live_count2 + (1|Replicate), data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m5b)

m6b <-glmmTMB(sed_dep_av ~ Treatmentf + Elevation + Live_count2 + (1|Replicatef), data = dat3, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
summary(m6b)


```

###Model Selection
```{r AIC}

AIC(m0a, m0b, m1b, m2b, m3b, m4b, m5b, m6b) %>%
  arrange(AIC) %>%
  print()

#m1b had the lowest AIC at -620

```

###Diagnostic plots to check model assumptions
```{r}

performance::check_model(m1b)
check_overdispersion(m1b) #no overdispersion detected so that is not why the variance is not spread evenly
#Homogeneity of variance is not good. It is very squiggly and not evenly spread. 

#Is there a better type of model I can use for this type of data?


```

###Model Predictions
```{r}
# use the ggpredict function in the ggeffects package to get estimated adjusted predictions and confidence intervals for each species at different levels of species

m1b_ggpredict <- 
  ggeffects::ggpredict(m1b, terms = c("Treatmentf"))

print(m1b_ggpredict, n = Inf)

plot(m1b_ggpredict) # default interaction plot; can use ggplot syntax to modify as needed

#make a better plot 
m1b_fig <- ggplot(m1b_ggpredict, aes(x = x, y = predicted))+
  geom_point(size = 3)+
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), width = 0.2)+
  geom_point(data = dat3, aes(x = Treatmentf, y = sed_dep_av, color = Treatmentf), inherit.aes = FALSE)+ 
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Sediment Deposition g/cm2/year"
    )+
  theme_classic()

print(m1b_fig)

#still need to change treatment names for the graph
```
